The [theory page](theory-and-mechanism.qmd) describes Dantzig–Wolfe decomposition
[@dantzig1960] and the column-generation loop that solves its master problem
[@fordfulkerson1958; @gilmore1961]. Stated that way, the loop is simple. In practice,
whether it is fast depends on a handful of recurring issues, collected here. The survey
of @lubbecke2005 covers them in depth, with an emphasis on the dual point of view.

## Tailing-off

Column generation often finds a near-optimal solution quickly, then spends many
iterations proving optimality. Throughout, the duals $\pi$ oscillate from iteration to
iteration. The [worked example](theory-and-mechanism.qmd#a-worked-example) on the theory
page shows this on a small scale: its Lagrangian lower bound is not monotone, because
the prices jump between iterations.

**Stabilization** fights this by keeping the duals near a good point, for example by
penalizing moves away from it [@dumerle1999].

## Early termination

Every iteration provides the Lagrangian lower bound $z_{\text{RMP}} + \sum_k
\min(0, \mathrm{rc}_k^\ast)$ [@geoffrion1974] as well as the upper bound $z_{\text{RMP}}$
(see [the theory page](theory-and-mechanism.qmd#column-generation-the-algorithm)). So
one can stop as soon as the gap between the two is small. In branch-and-price
[@desrosiers1984; @barnhart1998], this is often enough to prune a node without solving
its master to optimality.

## Initialization

The first restricted master problem must be feasible. In practice one adds artificial
columns with a high cost (a big-M "Phase I") or starts from a heuristic solution.

## Degeneracy

Master problems are often highly degenerate, with many dual optima for the same primal
solution, which also slows convergence [@lubbecke2005].
